notes.label: Framing word order
notes.trans: by such traps and the skill of lying Sinon
notes.body: talibus ... Sinonis frames the line, with the treachery woven through it, which reflects the web of lies Sinon spun around the Trojans.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.trans: taken in by tricks and forced tears
notes.body: The repeated hard c sounds in capti ... coactis make the line sound harsh, which stresses how cruelly the Trojans were fooled.

notes.label: Epithet
notes.body: Achilles is called "of Larisa", after a town in Thessaly near his home, a grand epic way of naming him that stresses how great a warrior he was.

notes.label: Anaphora
notes.trans: not ten years, not a thousand ships
notes.body: non is repeated at the start of each phrase, which piles up everything that failed to take Troy, so the success of one liar seems all the more shameful.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: Cf. Aescylus Agamemnon 45 - στόλον Ἀργείων χιλιοναύτην

notes.label: Tetracolon
notes.body: Four great forces, two heroes, ten years and a thousand ships, are listed, and all failed where Sinon succeeded, which makes his trick seem shocking.

notes.label: Comparative
notes.body: maius, "greater", warns that something worse than Sinon's lie is coming, so the reader braces for disaster.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The repeated m sounds in maius miseris multoque slow the line down, which builds a sense of dread.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: magis is moved to the start of line 200, away from tremendum, which stresses how much more frightening the new event is.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense turbat makes the panic feel as if it is happening now, which draws the reader into the scene.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: Laocoon was a priest of Apollo, but on this occasion was taking the place of the dead priest of Neptune

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: sacerdos ends the line, which stresses Laocoön's holy role and makes what happens to him all the more shocking.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: sollemnis and aras frame the line, so the sacrifice is enclosed by the holy altars, which makes the attack that follows a violation of something sacred.

notes.label: Imperfect tense
notes.body: The imperfect mactabat shows the sacrifice was still going on, so the serpents interrupt a holy act.

notes.label: Note

notes.label: Note

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: gemini (line 203) and angues (line 204) are far apart, with Aeneas' shudder in between, so the serpents are named only at the end, which builds suspense.

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: incumbunt pelago runs on from the line before, so the serpents seem to surge forward across the line break.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense brings the serpents vividly before the reader's eyes.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: the creatures ‘lean forward over the sea’ like rowers: a fine vivid word to express both movement and effort.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: tendunt continues the run of present tenses, so the serpents' steady approach feels immediate.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: undas ends its clause before the strong pause, which leaves the picture of the crests towering over the waves.

notes.label: Sibilance
notes.body: The hissing s sounds in sanguineae superant undas imitate the hissing of the serpents and the rush of the sea.

notes.label: Sinon
notes.body: A Greek left behind on purpose. Pretending to have escaped from his own side, he told the Trojans that the horse was an offering to Minerva (see the background panel below).

notes.label: Diomedes
notes.body: Diomedes, son of Tydeus, one of the bravest Greek warriors at Troy. Naming a hero by his father is a common feature of epic.

notes.label: Achilles
notes.body: The greatest of the Greek warriors at Troy; he killed Hector, but was himself killed before the city fell.

questions: How does Virgil make the serpents frightening in lines 203–207?
Why do you think Laocoön is shown in the middle of a sacrifice when the serpents arrive?
Lines 196–198 compare Sinon with the greatest Greek heroes. What point is Aeneas making?

context.body: The set text skips lines 57 to 194. In them, shepherds drag in a young Greek with his hands tied: Sinon. He tells the Trojans a carefully made-up story. He says the Greeks were about to sacrifice him, that he escaped, and that he now hates them. The horse, he claims, is an offering to Minerva to make up for the theft of her sacred statue, the Palladium, and it was built huge on purpose so that the Trojans could not take it into their city: if they did, Troy would one day defeat Greece. Priam believes him and has his bonds cut. The second passage begins as the Trojans accept the lie.
